Un océan de rails, de wagons-citernes et: An ocean of rails, tank wagons and ballast. In the middle, a signal box that someone still lives in.

Un village fortifié derrière des remorqu: A village fortified behind trailers and sandbags. There is soup and there are beds. There is always a price.

Entre les morts et les rails: Between the Dead and the Rails

Un tir patient qui ne rate jamais : crit: A patient shot that never misses: enhanced critical (×2.6 against a distracted or stunned target) and bleeding.

Des années aux urgences de l’hôpital Del: Years in the emergency department at Delorme Hospital, then fourteen months in a besieged pharmacy.
Elle connaît chaque galerie sous Valombr: She knows every tunnel beneath Valombre and every way of not being seen.

Armand gave me the key to his handcar. He took it from around his neck the way you take off a wedding ring.
Lucien cogne toujours, au bout de la voi: Lucien is still knocking, at the end of the siding. Armand says it’s better that way: he can still hear him, but from a distance.

I still have silt under my nails. The apple trees were blossoming in the water, and under the water there were people waiting.
Claire et Jules sont devant nous, quelqu: Claire and Jules are ahead of us, somewhere on the road. The little boy salutes backwards. I don’t think I’ll ever forget it.
Nour a porté le métronome tout le chemin: Nour carried the metronome the whole way. She was counting the beats, and for once she wasn’t counting to be less afraid.

Le petit a tenu son salut jusqu’à ce que: The little boy held his salute until the trees hid him. I keep telling myself we didn’t have time. I’ll keep telling myself that for a long time.

Kaz lisait l’eau comme un livre. Son pèr: Kaz read the water like a book. His father used to clear ditches. It’s the first time he has told me about his father.
Quatorze mois que ces voitures attendent: Fourteen months these cars have been waiting for the jam to clear. There are still people inside, belted in, waiting with them.
J’ai payé le tiers. Mon nom est écrit da: I paid the third. My name is written in a register, in capitals, between a wedding ring and a pair of shoes. Paid in full.

J’ai abattu le Péage. « Faut bien que qu: I shot down the Toll. “Someone has to keep the books.” I think he really meant it.
I crossed the viaduct through its belly. Those who hadn’t paid were still there, standing in the dark with their suitcases.
J’ai donné la voix de Rousset à un homme: I gave Rousset’s voice to a man who wants to use it to get on board the barge. I hope I haven’t sold the only proof we had.
Le gué de la Sauldre. C’est là que le ca: The Sauldre Ford. That’s where the lorry will deliver Théo. I read it in a register, between two lines of tinned food.
Ce soir, une cloche a sonné sur une coll: Tonight a bell rang on a hill. Just once. As if to say someone is still there.

Douze ardoises, douze prénoms à la craie: Twelve slates, twelve first names in chalk. I can’t decide whether Mother Agathe is the last sane person in the world, or the first to have gone mad.

Théo a dit non, ou c’est moi qui l’ai di: Théo said no, or I said it for him. I’m no longer sure which of the two he holds against me.
J’ai tué Frère Paul, le jardinier. Cléme: I killed Brother Paul, the gardener. Clémence is alive. Agathe thanked me and didn’t forgive me, and she was right twice over.
Frère Paul est retourné à son pilier. Il: Brother Paul went back to his pillar. It was raining when the gate closed, and he was looking at the cellar window.
Mes derniers antibiotiques sont dans le: My last antibiotics are in Sister Bénédicte’s blood. I may not get any more. She waved to me from the archway, and that was worth the box.
Bénédicte attendait près du treizième an: Bénédicte was waiting by the thirteenth ring when I left the priory. I had nothing to give her.
Nour est restée là-haut. Elle a compté m: Nour stayed up there. She counted my steps until the bend. I’ll have to retrace them the other way.
J’ai promis de revenir. Je ne sais pas e: I promised to come back. I don’t know yet whether it’s a promise or a prayer.
Nous avons dormi dans la tour du barrage: We slept in the tower of Vaulx Dam, above a black lake that makes no sound.
L’Institut a coupé le courant exprès. «: The Institute cut the power on purpose. “A lock with no power can be held by four men.” I didn’t think you could switch off a valley by calculation.
The shift supervisor was called L. Marchal. He had written “someone has to stay”. He stayed.
Les lampadaires se sont allumés le long: The streetlights came on along the river, one by one, all the way to Morvan. For a minute, I thought the world was going to come back with them.
The fuse cracked in my hands. Morvan will stay in the dark, and Rousset will be the one turning the cranks.
Je n’ai pas réarmé la ligne de Morvan. I: I didn’t reset the Morvan line. There are doors you don’t dare open, even when you know how.
Kaz m’a parlé d’Irena. Elle disait que l: Kaz told me about Irena. She used to say the dam purred like a cat.
Les lampadaires éclairent la route où ro: The streetlights light up the road Théo’s lorry is driving along. I don’t know if that’s any consolation.
Un convoi dans un fossé, au bord de la D: A convoy in a ditch, beside the D12. They called it “collection”. The word is embroidered on the sleeves.
J’ai dans ma poche un ordre signé du cap: In my pocket I have an order signed by Captain Rousset. “Priority: young subjects.” I read it three times. It doesn’t change.
Léa, Samuel, Inès, Noé, Jade, Tom, Lina,: Léa, Samuel, Inès, Noé, Jade, Tom, Lina, Hugo, Rayan, Zoé, Malo, Adam. I copied them out. I don’t know what became of them.
J’ai promis à Théo qu’il ne monterait ja: I promised Théo he would never get into a cage. He told me I couldn’t promise that. He’s right. I promised anyway.
Théo a mesuré la cage du bout avec son c: Théo measured the end cage with his pencil. It was his size. I told him the truth, and he thanked me the way you thank a doctor.
Quelque part sur une autre route, Théo e: Somewhere on another road, Théo is in a cage like those. I know it, and I keep walking in the same direction as him.
Mérel a fait hurler son ambulance pour n: Mérel set his ambulance wailing for us. I didn’t hear the end. I think he’d been waiting for it since January.
J’ai pris les antibiotiques qu’un homme: I took the antibiotics a man was keeping for children who won’t be coming back. I tell myself they’ll be of use. I tell myself that often.
Nous avons contourné le convoi. Il y a d: We went round the convoy. There are things you don’t have the strength to look at on the sixth day.
Le marais ne fait pas de bruit. C’est ce: The marsh makes no sound. That’s what frightened me most: not the teeth, the silence between the teeth.
La tourbe a voulu l’un des nôtres. Je ne: The peat wanted one of us. I didn’t let it have them.
J’ai mis trop longtemps à tirer. La tour: I took too long to shoot. The peat kept something to remember us by.
The peat took me up to my chest. No one saw me get out. No one would have seen me not get out.
Dans la cabane, une femme avait dessiné: In the hut, a woman had drawn birds, then people standing in the water. She called them the ramblers.
J’ai tué la Dame des tourbières. Elle po: I killed the Lady of the Bogs. She wore binoculars around her neck.
Nous sommes passés à côté d’elle. Elle a: We passed right by her. She is still waiting. I wonder what for.
J’ai laissé la cloche au marais. Je saur: I left the bell to the marsh. I’ll find out at the lock whether I was wrong.
Un camion, au loin, sur la route du fleu: A lorry in the distance, on the river road. I couldn’t take my eyes off it.
Une main de cambouis sur une porte. Gasp: A greasy handprint on a door. Gaspard is walking ahead of us, alone.
Brennes avait une fontaine qui coulait,: Brennes had a fountain that ran, a school, hot soup. For an hour, I believed the world still knew how to be kind.
Une soupe de poireaux qui sentait la poi: Leek soup that smelled of pear. I don’t think I’ll ever be able to sit at a table again without looking at the pots.
Le sirop m’a pris comme une vague. Je me: The syrup took me like a wave. I remember Vautrin’s smile, and thinking it was kind. That’s what frightens me.
Théo a montré sa cicatrice à une fille q: Théo showed his scar to a girl who had the same one. They didn’t say anything to each other. They didn’t need to.
Personne n’a frappé Vautrin. Il est part: No one hit Vautrin. He left with his suitcase, and the village watched him go the way you watch a storm pass.
On a fui par les rails. Elsa et Samuel s: We fled along the rails. Elsa and Samuel were left behind a new padlock. I count the hours that remain, and I count that too.
Elsa et Samuel sont dans une cave, derri: Elsa and Samuel are in a cellar, behind jars of beans. It isn’t much. It’s better than a hold.
« Ici Brennes. Nous ne livrerons personn: “This is Brennes. We will hand no one over.” Rousset knows we’re coming. Perhaps that’s for the best. Let him be afraid too.
J’ai arraché les lampes de la radio. Que: I ripped the valves out of the radio. Somewhere in Morvan, someone is waiting for a delivery that will never come.
La draisine d’Armand est là où il l’avai: Armand’s handcar is where he said it would be, under its green tarpaulin. The old man didn’t lie. I owe him that.
La ligne du fleuve. Des kilomètres de ra: The river line. Kilometres of rails that no longer lead anywhere, except to Morvan.
La draisine d’Armand file comme un chien: Armand’s handcar races along like a dog let off the lead. The river wind made my eyes water, and for once it was only the wind.
Elle a déraillé dans une courbe. J’ai en: It derailed on a bend. I heard the axle twist. Her name was Odette. I won’t dare tell Armand.
Des heures sur le ballast. Les traverses: Hours on the ballast. The sleepers are never the right distance apart for a human stride. I think they were laid for trains, not for us.
Le 6142 était couché dans les ronces, la: The 6142 lay in the brambles, its door torn off from the inside. Eleven passengers. I didn’t try to find out what became of them.
Jules a fait le salut à l’envers au fleu: Jules gave his backwards salute to the river, to the dead cows in the fields, to me. Claire didn’t smile. But she put her suitcase down for a while.
Il y a une cage sous une bâche, en bas,: There’s a cage under a tarpaulin, down at the ford. I know who is inside. He is two hundred metres from me.
Gaspard Lenoir, assis sur une borne, san: Gaspard Lenoir, sitting on a bollard, no paint on his face. He looked like any old man. Maybe that’s what he always was.
Le pont de la Sauldre est couché dans l’: The Sauldre bridge lies in the water. We crossed on foot, on stones someone laid there two hundred years ago.
Théo est sorti de sa cage avec un clou d: Théo came out of his cage with a nail in his pocket. He had scratched the way back into the floorboards. He walks two steps behind me. I don’t ask him to come closer.
J’ai vu Théo dans une cage, au milieu d’: I saw Théo in a cage, in the middle of a river, and I watched him go. I have no excuse. I’ve stopped looking for one.
Lou, Samuel, Aurélie. J’écris leurs noms: Lou, Samuel, Aurélie. I write their names so they exist somewhere other than on a delivery note.
Il y avait deux enfants dans des cages e: There were two children in cages and I did nothing. I keep telling myself we wouldn’t have won. I can’t make myself believe it.
Les hommes de la barge ont des combinais: The barge men wear grey coveralls and speak with ticket-counter voices. Now they know we’re coming.
Gaspard Lenoir a pris une balle pour des: Gaspard Lenoir took a bullet for children he would have sold a week ago. I don’t know what to make of that.
Le jeune soldat courait vers sa radio. I: The young soldier was running for his radio. He didn’t make it. I tell myself it was him or us. It’s true. It isn’t enough.
J’écris dans une chapelle sans toit, à l: I’m writing in a roofless chapel, by the glow of the barge’s searchlights. You can see them from here. They sweep all night long.
The streetlights of Morvan are on. A lit street. I had forgotten how beautiful that is.
Maëlle m’a montré sa peur, ce soir. Une: Maëlle showed me her fear tonight. For a second. It moved me more than all her thank-yous.
Théo a dessiné la mer : une seule ligne,: Théo drew the sea: a single line, very long. He wants to be asked. It isn’t much, and it’s everything he has been denied.
Kaz once lived in the house with the blue shutters. He says twelve minutes is a long time. I don’t like the way he said it.
Inès thinks there’s too much sky here. She doesn’t know whether she’ll go on board. For once she doesn’t know, and she says so.
Nour m’a dit son nom de famille. Je ne l: Nour told me her surname. I’m not writing it down. I promised.
Nour compte tout : les pas, les plaques,: Nour counts everything: steps, plates, hours. I think she also counts the adults she can trust. The number is small.
Gaspard Lenoir a dormi à notre feu. Il y: Gaspard Lenoir slept by our fire. A week ago, I would have killed him for less.
Jules m’a fait son salut à l’envers avan: Jules gave me his backwards salute before falling asleep on the suitcase. Claire was playing a sonata on her knees.
Quelque part devant nous, il y a un cami: Somewhere ahead of us, there’s a lorry and a cage. Tomorrow I’ll see Théo. I don’t know if he’ll want to look at me.
Demain, je parlerai d’abord. J’ai mes pr: Tomorrow, I’ll talk first. I have my proof held against my chest.
Demain, s’ils trient, on ne se laissera: Tomorrow, if they sort us, we won’t let ourselves be sorted. I checked the weapons twice.
Demain, on regarde avant d’agir. Toute g: Tomorrow, we look before we act. Every fence has a weak spot. You just need the time to find it.
Demain, c’est Théo qui parlera. Mon seul: Tomorrow, Théo will do the talking. My only job will be to make sure he’s heard.

Vous avez laissé tomber le vieil aiguill: You let down the old signalman of the Outskirts.
Vous avez descendu Claire et Jules Delma: You brought Claire and Jules Delmas down from their roof, in the middle of the Drowned Orchards.
Vous avez laissé Claire et Jules Delmas: You left Claire and Jules Delmas on their roof.
Vous avez payé le Péage pour passer la r: You paid the Toll to get across the Ring Road.

Vous avez contourné le Péage par le viad: You got round the Toll by way of the viaduct.
Théo a donné son sang aux pensionnaires: Théo gave his blood to the priory’s residents.
Le prieuré de Saint-Aubin vous a promis: Saint-Aubin Priory promised you a refuge.
Vous avez rendu le courant au barrage de: You restored the power at Vaulx Dam.
Vous avez trouvé l’ordre de mission sign: You found the mission order signed by Rousset in the wreck of the convoy.
Vous avez traversé les tourbières sans r: You crossed the Peat Bogs without waking the Lady.
Vous avez démasqué le maire de Brennes d: You unmasked the mayor of Brennes in front of his village.
Vous avez descendu la ligne du fleuve su: You rode down the river line on Armand’s handcar.
Vous avez ouvert la cage de Théo au gué: You opened Théo’s cage at the Sauldre Ford.
Vous aviez vendu Théo. Vous l’avez repri: You had sold Théo. You took him back. He hasn’t forgotten.
Vous avez libéré les captifs de la livra: You freed the captives of the delivery at the ford.
Le courant de Vaulx a ouvert les portes: The power from Vaulx opened the lock gates.
Les lampadaires du quai sont allumés. Le: The quayside street lamps are lit. The power you gave back to Vaulx Dam has made it all the way here, and no one in this crowd knows where it comes from.
Les vannes de l’écluse ont du courant, c: The lock’s sluices have power, the power from Vaulx: the motors can open them without a crank.
Quelqu’un vous attrape la manche. Claire: Someone catches your sleeve. Claire Delmas. You brought her down from a roof, in the middle of the Drowned Orchards, with her son and her suitcase. She kept her word: she made it all the way here. Jules is asleep against her shoulder, his cheeks too red.
« Ce n’est pas la Fièvre, souffle-t-elle: “It isn’t the Fever,” she breathes. “He cut his hand open on the barbed wire last night, trying to get through the fence. They don’t take the sick.” She doesn’t ask you for anything. She told you so already, on the roof: she never asks for anything.
Au premier rang, une femme serre un enfa: In the front row, a woman holds a six-year-old child tight against her. Claire Delmas. You left her on her roof, in the middle of the orchards. She came anyway, alone, on foot. She recognises you. She doesn’t look away.
Little Jules’s cheeks are too red. “A cut,” she says, though you haven’t asked anything. “It isn’t the Fever. But they don’t take the sick.”
Poser sur la caisse l’ordre de mission d: Lay the Convoy’s mission order, signed by Captain Rousset, on the crate.
Pour quitter l’écluse, la Destinée doit: To leave the lock, the Destinée has to go down into the basin and wait for the downstream gates to open. The power from Vaulx has made it all the way here: in the lock-keeper’s house, at the edge of the path, the sluice motors can run on their own. Slowly. And the house is where the horde will arrive first.
Six minutes de moteur, ou douze de maniv: Six minutes on the motors, or twelve on the crank if the power trips. Someone has to hold the door.
Lancer les moteurs des vannes avec le co: Start the sluice motors with the power from Vaulx, and hold the door of the house while they run.
Le courant du barrage de Vaulx a ouvert: The power from Vaulx Dam opened the lock gates.
La porte de la maison a cédé. Le Colosse: The door of the house gave way. The Colossus walked into the light of the motors.
Claire Delmas donne des leçons de piano: Claire Delmas gives piano lessons on a keyboard with no strings, painted on a plank. Her pupils swear you can still hear the music.
Armand Vidal fait toujours rouler sa dra: Armand Vidal still runs his handcar along the river line. He has repainted “Odette” on its side, in fresh lettering.
À la gare de triage, Armand Vidal a rall: At the marshalling yard, Armand Vidal has lit the stove in the signal box again. He is still waiting for the 6142. He no longer waits alone.
Le barrage de Vaulx tourne encore. Le lo: Vaulx Dam is still running. All along the river, every night, a line of street lamps comes on for those who walk.
Mère Agathe garde la porte du prieuré ou: Mother Agathe keeps the priory door open. The crypt, though, stays shut, and the sisters go on washing those who are kept there.
Brennes a élu un nouveau maire. La premi: Brennes has elected a new mayor. The council’s first decision was to close for good the classroom where the “medical check-ups” were held.
Au gué de la Sauldre, quelqu’un a planté: At the Sauldre Ford, someone has planted a wooden cross for every cage that was opened. There are a great many.
Vous montrez la plaque de Gaspard. On vo: You show Gaspard’s tag. You are taken aboard with the delivery, no questions asked. The cages in the lorry are empty: you opened them at the Sauldre Ford. Théo didn’t come aboard. He watched you hold out the tag, and he set off back along the towpath.
L’aqueduc vous recrache dans un fossé de: The aqueduct spits you out into a bramble-choked ditch at the foot of a dry-stone wall. Night is falling. After three days beneath the city, the open air tastes of iron and wet grass, and the sky seems too big.
Derrière le mur commence le cimetière Sa: Beyond the wall lies Saint-Lazare Cemetery. Black cypresses, crooked crosses, family vaults with cast-iron doors gaping open. Further on, you can make out the embankments of the marshalling yard, then the slope running down to the port.
Entre les tombes, des silhouettes. Huit,: Between the graves, figures. Eight, perhaps more. They stand in the paths without moving, heads tilted slightly, like people who came to lay flowers on a grave and forgot which one. The wind carries the clicking of their teeth to you.
« Huit. Deux près de la chapelle, trois: “Eight. Two by the chapel, three on the central path, the rest towards the north gate.” She counted without turning her head.
« Les morts qui gardent les morts », mur: “The dead guarding the dead,” Kaz murmurs. “There’s a certain logic to it.”
Théo s’est accroupi contre le mur. Il re: Théo has crouched against the wall. He looks at the cemetery the way he looks at everything: to make a map of it.
Théo n’est pas là. Vous vous surprenez à: Théo isn’t here. You catch yourself looking for his silhouette behind you, before you remember that he stayed with the Watchers, safe beneath the bones of Saint-Roch.
Personne ne marche à côté de vous. Le si: No one walks beside you. The silence is the same as underground, but here it has room to spread.
Traverser les allées en silence, de tomb: Cross the paths in silence, from grave to grave.
[Ancien cataphile] Passer sous le cimeti: [Cataphile] Go under the cemetery, through the ossuary of the abandoned plots.
Faire tinter la cloche du Berger contre: Ring the Shepherd’s bell against the east wall and let the Mutes go to the sound.
Longer le mur par l’extérieur, à travers: Skirt the wall on the outside, through the brambles.
Frapper les plus proches avant qu’ils se: Strike the nearest ones before they turn round.
Un gravier roule sous votre semelle. Les: A piece of gravel rolls under your sole. The heads turn towards you, one by one, with that slowness that is never quite slowness.
Deux Rôdeurs se détachent des tombes. Le: Two Prowlers break away from the graves. The others will follow if this drags on.

Un coup vous jette contre une stèle. Vou: A blow throws you against a headstone. You crawl, not knowing where, to a cast-iron door standing ajar. You pull it shut behind you and stay there, in the dark and the smell of cold stone.
Dehors, les dents claquent contre la por: Outside, teeth snap against the door. Then, very slowly, they move away. In the scramble, some of your supplies were left behind on the path.
Les Muets du cimetière vous ont repoussé: The cemetery’s Mutes drove you back into a vault.
Attendre que le cliquetis se soit éloign: Wait for the clicking to fade.
Le caveau de la famille Lafargue est une: The Lafargue family vault is a small granite chapel, with a smashed stained-glass window and four coffins stowed on shelves like suitcases on a night train. Someone has lived here. A foam mattress, candles melted onto a coffin lid, empty tins stacked with care.
Loin derrière vous, contre le mur est, l: Far behind you, against the east wall, the Mutes are still crowding round the spot where the bell rang.
Théo recopie les noms gravés dans la pie: Théo copies down the names carved in the stone. Lafargue Émile, Lafargue Jeanne, Lafargue Paul. “So someone will have written them down somewhere else,” he says.
Dans le caveau Lafargue : une ration, de: In the Lafargue vault: a ration, some rags, a bottle of calvados set on a coffin like an offering.
Les ronces vous ont lacéré les mains, et: The brambles have torn your hands, and it is pitch dark when you find the north gate again, from outside the wall.
Le long du portail, la terre a été retou: Along the gate, the earth has been turned over. Dozens of recent graves, without stones, each marked with a plank and a hand-painted name. The last ones have no plank: the names are written in grease pencil on the neighbours’ headstones.
La dernière fosse est vide. Une pelle es: The last grave is empty. A shovel stands planted in the mound of earth. On the plank, there is no name yet. Next to it, the keeper’s lodge, a brick hut with a corrugated-iron roof, its door ajar.
La grille du portail est ouverte. Une ch: The gate stands open. A chain and padlock hang from the bars, as if someone had meant to lock it and run out of time.
« Si on laisse ça ouvert, ils nous suivr: “If we leave that open, they’ll follow us all the way to the tracks,” says Inès.
Refermer la grille derrière vous avec la: Chain the gate shut behind you.
Go through the gate without wasting time.
The marshalling yard is a sea of rails. Thirty tracks side by side, rows of grey tank wagons that haven’t moved in fourteen months, and mist rising from the ditches up to the axles. The ballast crunches with every step. It smells of cold oil and turned earth.
Et dans le silence, un bruit. Un coup so: And in the silence, a sound. A dull, metallic, regular thud. Then another. Something is banging against the side of a tank wagon, from the inside, with a terrible patience.
« Citerne de quatre-vingts mètres cubes,: “Eighty-cubic-metre tank, four axles. It rings like a church bell. Whatever’s banging in there, you can hear it two kilometres away.”
Théo compte les voies à voix basse et le: Théo counts the tracks under his breath and draws them in pencil, in a single stroke, without lifting the lead.
Derrière vous, du côté du cimetière, le: Behind you, over by the cemetery, the ballast is crunching too. They found the gate open, and they are following the noise.
Au milieu des voies se dresse le poste d: In the middle of the tracks stands the signal box, a brick tower topped with a glazed cabin. Behind a pane, a candle. A window opens, and the barrel of a carbine comes to rest on the sill.
« Halte-là. Le 6142 a quatorze mois de r: “Halt. The 6142 is fourteen months late, and you’re not the 6142. So who are you?”
Dire que vous venez de chez les Veilleur: Say you’ve come from the Watchers of Saint-Roch, sent by Hélène.
Ne pas répondre. Filer entre les wagons,: Don’t answer. Slip between the wagons, towards the port embankment.
You won’t come back to the signal box.
Il vous fait monter par un escalier de f: He has you climb an iron staircase. The cabin is long and narrow. A row of big levers with red and blue handles, a track diagram where not a single bulb lights up any more, a calendar stopped at the month of the Fever. On the glass, a photo of a woman, wedged into the seal.
L’homme a soixante-dix ans, une casquett: The man is seventy, an SNCF cap jammed on his head and one leg stretched out on a chair, swaddled in a rag that smells bad. He holds his carbine the way you would hold a walking stick.
« Armand Vidal, aiguilleur, trente-huit: “Armand Vidal, signalman, thirty-eight years’ service. Sit down. Not there, that’s Odette’s chair.” He taps the glass towards the tracks. “The 6142 was the Lyon freight. It never set off again. I wait for it all the same. Someone has to wait for it.”
« Hélène ? Ses cloches passent par ici,: “Hélène? Her bells come through here, sometimes. She leaves me water at the foot of the stairs. If she sent you, you can’t be too bad.”
Le coup sourd, encore. Les vitres vibren: The dull thud, again. The windows shudder.
« Ça, c’est Lucien. Mon chef de manœuvre: “That’s Lucien. My shunting foreman. He went up to check a tank wagon, the last day, and he fell in, with the fever. He’s been banging since winter. I haven’t the heart. And he draws them, you see. Every night there are a few more of them round the box.”
« Votre jambe. » Ce n’est pas une questi: “Your leg.” It isn’t a question. Maëlle has already lifted the rag. “It’s not a bite. It’s dirty, and nobody has seen to it.”
Maëlle regarde la ligne rouge qui remont: Maëlle looks at the red line creeping up towards Armand’s knee. She had the same one, not so long ago. She says nothing, but she has already opened her bag.
Le poêle ronfle. Pour la première fois d: The stove roars. For the first time in a long while, no doubt, it is warm in the signal box.
Au poste d’aiguillage du triage vit Arma: In the marshalling yard’s signal box lives Armand Vidal, an old signalman who talks to trains.
Laisser Maëlle s’occuper de la jambe d’A: Let Maëlle see to Armand’s leg.
[Ancien ambulancier] Ouvrir l’abcès, net: [Paramedic] Lance the abscess, clean it, redo the dressing.
Nettoyer et panser la plaie avec votre t: Clean and dress the wound with your first-aid kit.
Give him your box of antibiotics.
Ce sont peut-être les seuls antibiotique: These may be the only antibiotics for miles.
Go and look at the tank wagon where Lucien is banging.
Remettre en état le poêle : le conduit e: Fix the stove: the flue is blocked and the door won’t shut.
Lui prendre ce qu’il a. Il est vieux, il: Take what he has. He’s old, he’s alone, and his leg is rotting.
Armand will no longer help you.
Attendre qu’il s’assoupisse, et fouiller: Wait for him to doze off, and search the signal box.
Vous avez volé Armand Vidal pendant son: You robbed Armand Vidal in his sleep.
Le remercier et repartir vers le remblai: Thank him and set off for the embankment.
Il faut ouvrir. Armand serre sa casquett: It has to be opened. Armand clamps his cap between his teeth as the blade goes in, and he doesn’t cry out. The pus runs, yellow and thick, smelling of rotten fruit. Then alcohol, compresses, a bandage pulled tight.
« Un clou rouillé, sur le ballast. Trois: “A rusty nail, on the ballast. Three weeks without treatment. One more and it would have been the leg. Two more and it would have been you.” She knots the bandage with a sharp tug. “Keep it raised. And drink. Water.”
« Odette disait toujours que j’étais dou: “Odette always said I was a baby about pain.” He wipes his eyes with the back of his hand. “She’d have been disappointed.”
Armand décolle la photo de la vitre avec: Armand peels the photo off the glass with the delicacy of a bomb-disposal expert. A plump woman in a yellow oilskin, on a handcar, laughing as she holds on to her hat.
« Garde-barrière au passage à niveau de: “Level-crossing keeper at Brennes. Forty years. She raised the barrier for the tractors and lowered it for me. That’s how we met: I came through four times a day, and in the end, I stopped.”
« Le dimanche, on prenait la draisine su: “On Sundays we’d take the handcar out on the river line, with a picnic. She loved speed. Me, I was scared, but I never said.” He sets the photo face down on the desk. “The Fever took her the first week. We buried her at Saint-Lazare, Fernand and me. Fernand’s the gravedigger. I don’t know what became of him.”
« Tiens. » Il sort d’un tiroir deux bâto: “Here.” From a drawer he takes two red sticks with caps. “Track flares. Odette always kept some in her oilskin. To stop a train. Or to make people look the other way.”
Lui dire que vous avez lu son nom dans l: Tell him you read her name in Fernand’s register.
La citerne est sur la voie 12, au milieu: The tank wagon stands on track 12, in the middle of a rake of six. Its grey side is dented from the inside, dozens of small round bulges, at head height. The loading dome on top is closed with a cast-iron handwheel. With each blow, rust falls in a fine snow onto the ballast.
« Le volant du dôme se dévisse à la main: “The dome wheel unscrews by hand. The drain valve at the bottom is too small for him.” He lays his palm on the side, and the next blow makes it tremble. “But look at the track: it slopes down to the siding. If we slacken the screw brakes and uncouple the wagon, it’ll roll on its own to the buffer stop. Down there, it’ll bang for nobody.”
Les freins à vis sont serrés sur chaque: The screw brakes are clamped tight on every axle. The track slopes gently down towards the far end of the yard, where the buffer stops of the siding loom in the mist.
Là-haut, à la fenêtre du poste, la silho: Up above, at the signal-box window, Armand’s silhouette doesn’t move.
Desserrer les freins, décrocher la citer: Release the brakes, uncouple the tank wagon and push it towards the siding.
Ouvrir le dôme sans un bruit pendant qu’: Open the dome without a sound while Inès aims at the opening.
Dévisser le dôme et l’attendre, arme à l: Unscrew the dome and wait for him, weapon in hand.
The dome gives with a clang like a saucepan. Lucien comes out like a swimmer surfacing, in faded work overalls, his nails torn off from all the banging. He drops onto the ballast on all fours, and he runs.
Le chef de manœuvre jaillit de la citern: The shunting foreman bursts out of the tank. Fourteen months shut in haven’t slowed him down.
The dome gives with a clang like a saucepan. Lucien comes out like a swimmer surfacing, in faded work overalls. And the racket raises other shadows between the wagons: the ones from the cemetery, who came through the gate you left open and followed your tracks to the rails.
Lucien, et deux Rôdeurs venus de Saint-L: Lucien, and two Prowlers from Saint-Lazare. The open gate costs you dearly.
Vous tombez à la renverse sur le ballast: You fall backwards onto the ballast. Lucien is on top of you, his teeth a breath from your throat. Then a shot cracks out, so loud it rolls across the whole yard like thunder, and the weight slumps to one side.
Là-haut, à la fenêtre, Armand baisse sa: Up at the window, Armand lowers his carbine. He fired himself, in the end. He stays a long time without moving, his cheek against the stock.
Au loin, du côté du port, une lampe s’al: In the distance, towards the port, a lamp comes on atop a crane. The shot has been heard.
Armand a abattu Lucien lui-même pour vou: Armand shot Lucien himself to save you. The shot carried all the way to the port.
Limp back up to the signal box.
Les freins se desserrent avec un cri de: The brakes come loose with a shriek of rust. You brace your shoulders against the buffer, and the tank wagon lurches, a centimetre, then a metre. It moves off into the mist, grinding, faster and faster. Long afterwards, a heavy impact: the buffer stop. Then, very far away, little knocks, almost nothing.
À la fenêtre du poste, Armand a ôté sa c: At the signal-box window, Armand has taken off his cap.
Lucien est étendu sur le ballast, le vis: Lucien lies on the ballast, face against the stones. A laminated badge still hangs from his overalls: L. Marchetti, shunting foreman. Armand comes down the iron staircase one step at a time, on his bad leg, a wagon tarpaulin under his arm.
“Thirty years we worked together. He never called me anything but ‘the old man’.” He spreads the tarpaulin over the body and weighs it down with ballast stones. “Thank you for doing it in my place.”
Le silence qui suit est si vaste qu’on e: The silence that follows is so vast you can hear the mist dripping from the wagons.
The tank wagon on track 12 has stopped banging.
Climb back up to the signal box.
Le plancher craque sous votre genou, prè: The floorboard creaks under your knee, near the chest. Armand opens his eyes. He wasn’t really asleep; at his age, you never really sleep any more.
Vous faites un pas vers lui. Il ne recul: You take a step towards him. He doesn’t back away. He has nowhere to back away to.
La carabine se relève. Il ne tire pas su: The carbine comes up. He doesn’t shoot at you. He puts the barrel out of the window and fires into the air, once. The shot rolls across the whole marshalling yard, all the way to the quays, and a lamp comes on at the top of a crane in the port.
« Dehors. La prochaine, elle est pour to: “Out. The next one’s for you. And if you meet any trains, tell them the signalman isn’t there for anyone any more.”
Théo vous regarde comme on regarde quelq: Théo looks at you the way you look at someone for the first time.
Maëlle descend l’escalier la première, s: Maëlle goes down the stairs first, without a word, without waiting for you.
Vous avez brusqué Armand Vidal. Son coup: You roughed up Armand Vidal. His warning shot alerted the port.
Head down to the embankment, fast.
Vous lui récitez la ligne. « Odette Vida: You recite the line to him. “Odette Vidal, retired level-crossing keeper. Her husband held the shovel with me.” And you tell him the last one too, the one where Fernand wrote his own name, and about the empty grave by the gate.
Armand ne dit rien pendant longtemps. Pu: Armand says nothing for a long time. Then he turns the photo the right way up and wedges it back into the seal of the glass.
« Il a tenu plus longtemps que moi, alor: “He held out longer than me, then. He buried the whole neighbourhood, and I stayed up here waiting for a train.” He sniffs. “Thank you for telling me. You think you’d rather not know. It’s not true.”
Armand se tait un long moment. Puis il d: Armand is silent for a long moment. Then he undoes his shirt collar and pulls a chain from round his neck. On the end hangs a railwayman’s T-key, worn down to the copper, engraved “A.V. — Brennes”.
« Ma draisine est à Brennes, dans la rem: “My handcar is at Brennes, in the station shed, under the green tarpaulin. She pulls a bit to the left, like me. On the river line, she’ll save you half a day. I won’t be driving her again.” He puts the key in your hand and closes your fingers over it.
« C’était notre draisine, à Odette et mo: “It was our handcar, Odette’s and mine. It makes me glad she’ll run again.”
« Et prends ça. Ma réserve, sous le plan: “And take this. My stash, under the floor. I couldn’t bend down to reach it any more.” He hands you a tin and two wrapped ship’s biscuits.
Il tend à Théo un vieux plan plié de la: He hands Théo an old folded map of the river line, covered in pencil notes. “You draw tracks, you do. Learn this one by heart.” Théo tucks it into his jacket, close to his chest.
« Au petit jour, quand vous serez sur le: “At first light, when you’re on the embankment, I’ll throw the number 4 points. They’ve always squealed like a stuck pig. The lot in the crane will look this way. That’ll give you a minute. A minute is a long time, on an embankment.”
Armand Vidal vous a confié la clé de sa: Armand Vidal has entrusted you with the key to his handcar, stored at Brennes station.
Dormir quelques heures pendant qu’Armand: Sleep a few hours while Armand keeps watch.
Feuilleter le cahier de service posé sur: Leaf through the service log on the desk.
Head down to the embankment before daybreak.
L’aube vient sans couleur. La voie quitt: Dawn comes without colour. The track leaves the yard and runs down to the quays on a long ballast embankment, lined by a rake of covered wagons halted there for good. Below, the port: cranes, warehouse roofs, the pewter-coloured river.
Au sommet de la grue la plus proche, deu: At the top of the nearest crane, two Scrappers are passing a cigarette back and forth in the cab. A two-man patrol strolls up the ballast, rifle on shoulder, and back down. Always the same route.
La patrouille ne se promène plus. Les de: The patrol is no longer strolling. The two men are searching the ballast by lamplight, facing the yard, where the shot came from.
« Deux dans la grue, deux sur la voie. I: “Two in the crane, two on the track. They take four minutes to go up and come back down. They never look under the wagons.” She counted three times before speaking.
Kaz regarde la grue. Il connaît ces gens: Kaz looks at the crane. He knows those people; he must have stood them drinks, before. He says nothing.
Dans la cabine de la grue, une grande si: In the crane cab, a tall figure stands up and shoulders a metre-long monkey wrench. You know that build.
La ration volée à Armand pèse dans votre: The ration you stole from Armand weighs in your bag. It weighs more than a ration should.
Attendre que l’aiguille du 4 hurle, là-h: Wait for the number 4 points to squeal, up in the yard, as Armand promised.
Lancer une fusée de voie loin sur les ra: Throw a track flare far down the rails so the crane looks the other way.
[Ancien pompier] Passer sous le remblai: [Firefighter] Go under the embankment through the storm-drain culvert.
Ramper sous les wagons jusqu’au bas du r: Crawl under the wagons to the bottom of the embankment.
Ramper sous les wagons, malgré la patrou: Crawl under the wagons, despite the patrol on the alert.
Attendre la patrouille entre deux wagons: Wait for the patrol between two wagons and take it from behind.
Un caillou de ballast roule sous votre c: A ballast stone rolls from under your elbow and tumbles down the bank. A lamp swings under the wagons. “Someone’s under there!”
Deux Ferrailleurs vous tirent de sous le: Two Scrappers drag you out from under the wagons. Be quick, before the crane gets involved.
Ils passent à votre hauteur en parlant d: They pass right by you, talking about a can of petrol. The first one only sees you when it’s too late.
Embuscade : la patrouille n’a rien vu ve: Ambush: the patrol never saw it coming.
Vous tirez les deux corps sous un wagon: You drag the two bodies under a wagon and cover them with a tarpaulin. In their pockets: cartridges, a ration, a flick knife, and a scrap of cardboard with the shift rota pencilled on it. Crane: two. Embankment: two. Quay: three. Someone at the port can count.
Personne n’a crié. Dans la cabine de la: No one cried out. In the crane cab, the cigarette still glows.
Descendre vers les quais avant la relève: Head down to the quays before the shift changes.
Une crosse vous cueille à la tempe. Vous: A rifle butt catches you on the temple. You roll to the bottom of the bank, into the water-filled ditch. Feet prod at you, a hand tears away whatever is sticking out of your bag. Someone says: “Leave it, it’s not breathing any more,” and the footsteps climb away.
C’est Kaz qui vous sort de l’eau, une ma: It’s Kaz who pulls you out of the water, a hand under each armpit, like a sack of cement.
C’est Inès qui vous trouve dans le fossé: It’s Inès who finds you in the ditch. She says nothing. She wipes your face with her sleeve.
Vous restez dans l’eau froide jusqu’à ce: You lie in the cold water until the light comes back. No one comes. That is a kind of luck in itself.
Une patrouille de Ferrailleurs vous a la: A Scrapper patrol left you for dead on the embankment.
Là-haut, au triage, une aiguille hurle c: Up in the yard, a set of points squeals like an animal having its throat cut. In the crane, both heads turn together. You hurtle down the embankment during that minute, and it is long, indeed.
La fusée se pose sur les rails dans une: The flare lands on the rails in a spray of red, far behind you. The whole crane watches it burn.
Vous sortez de la buse dans les roseaux,: You come out of the culvert into the reeds, knee-deep in water, twenty metres from the quay. No one ever looks underneath.
Vous vous cachez sous le plancher d’un h: You hide under the floor of a boathouse, level with the quay, among piles black with silt. Day breaks, grey. Mist trails over the river. You eat without a word, listening to the port wake up above you.
La clé d’Armand pend à votre cou, froide: Armand’s key hangs round your neck, cold against your skin. Brennes is far away. But it exists.
Vous repensez au vieil homme à sa fenêtr: You think back to the old man at his window, his carbine, his train that will never come. You won’t get the chance to ask his forgiveness.
Théo a sorti le plan d’Armand. Il y ajou: Théo has taken out Armand’s map. In pencil, he adds the marshalling yard, the embankment, the crane. Then he folds it up again and keeps it close.
Théo dessine le cimetière de mémoire : l: Théo draws the cemetery from memory: the paths, the cypresses, the empty grave by the gate.
Le groupe a traversé les Faubourgs et at: The group has crossed the Outskirts and reached the port of Valombre.
Les colonnes « concession » et « famille:
The “plot” and “family present” columns haven’t been filled in for a long time.

Ma Mathilde,\n\nLa digue a lâché le soir:
My Mathilde,

The dyke gave way on the evening of Martinmas. I heard it from here, like a door slamming a long way off. By morning, the orchard was a lake. The Reinettes at the bottom have water up to their first branches, the Belchards too. The old Calvilles, the ones your grandfather grafted, are on the mound. They’re holding.

There are things in the water. The Rabiers, the Morels, others I don’t recognise. They never come up onto the mound. I think they’ve forgotten how to climb. I don’t go down to the cellar any more.

Don’t come. I know you’d want to come. There are no more trains anyway, and you have the little ones.

I’m staying with the trees. They’ll blossom in April, there’ll be no one to prune them, and they’ll blossom anyway. That comforts me more than it should.

If someone reads this letter before you do: there are dried apples in the jar, take them. Leave the chair in front of the window.

Your dad,
Lucien Garnier

In front of the red-and-white barrier, a folding table, a kitchen scale, a ledger bound in green cloth.

The Toll, put out, applies the “house rate”: one ration, and let’s say no more about it.
Le Péage range la cassette dans la poche: The Toll tucks the cassette into the chest pocket of his overalls and zips it all the way up, the way you’d close a safe.

A box girder, as the engineers say: a long concrete corridor crossing the whole valley, with an inspection door at the top of the first pier, at the end of a caged ladder.
C’est la porte de service que vous aviez: It’s the service door you spotted through the binoculars. A chain, a rusty padlock. No one guards it.
« Un caisson de viaduc », dit Kaz en lev: “A viaduct box girder,” says Kaz, looking up. “I’ve been inside a few, for the canal. It’s pitch black in there, and everything that falls off the deck ends up inside. Everything.”

Longer la corniche extérieure, encordés: Edge along the outer ledge, roped to the railing.
Laisser Inès ouvrir la voie sur la corni: Let Inès lead the way along the ledge, as in the Quarries.
Longer la corniche sans corde, le ventre: Edge along the ledge without a rope, belly against the concrete.
Remonter sur l’autoroute et affronter la: Climb back up to the motorway and face the barrier.
Le cadenas cède. Derrière la porte, un c: The padlock gives. Behind the door, a rectangular corridor of raw concrete, two metres high, running straight into the dark. Nour compte à voix basse. « Cinquante-de: Nour counts under her breath. “Fifty-two. Fifty-three.” She will count all the way. It stops her being afraid, or it stops her showing it.

[Cataphile] Éteindre la lampe et passer: [Cataphile] Turn off the lamp and go by touch, one hand on the wall, as beneath Valombre.
Allumer une fusée de détresse et la jete: Light a distress flare and throw it far behind them, towards the entrance.
Passer entre eux, lampe masquée, en rete: Pass between them, lamp covered, holding your breath.

Une trappe dans la paroi, au-dessus d’un: A hatch in the wall, above a ladder, opens onto the embankment on the far side. Behind you, the toll plaza. Up there, no one has seen a thing.
« Il doit y avoir trois cents alliances: “There must be three hundred wedding rings in there,” says Maëlle. She doesn’t touch the jar.
Vous avez traversé le viaduc par l’intér: You crossed the viaduct through the inside of the box girder, without paying the toll.

Things are still falling, further down, for a long time, before they reach the river.

You fall into the next cell, ankle twisted, forehead split against a bulkhead. Above, someone slams the steel plate shut. Hands claw at the metal, then give up.

Limp to the edge of the road.
Le Péage soupire, comme devant un client: The Toll sighs, like a man facing a customer who disputes a bill. He gets up. He takes forever getting up. With one wrench he tears the red-and-white barrier off its pivot and weighs it in his hands, two metres of sheet metal and steel, which he holds like a shield.
« Personne ne tire », dit-il à ses homme: “Nobody shoots,” he tells his men. “This is a matter of accounting.”
Le Péage. Derrière sa barrière, il encai: The Toll. Behind his barrier he soaks up everything: wait for him to raise it, and make him drop his guard.

Vous remontez de la corniche par-dessus: You climb up from the ledge over the parapet, knuckles white and knees like jelly, just behind the toll plaza. The orange vests are all looking the other way, towards the ones who are coming.

Théo a ajouté le viaduc de la Rocade à s: Théo has added the Ring Road viaduct to his map. Under the deck, he has drawn the figures in the box girder.
Prendre la route qui descend vers la val: Take the road down towards the valley.
Au bas de la descente, vous faites halte: At the bottom of the descent, you stop under a slip-road bridge, out of the wind, and eat without speaking. The viaduct is nothing more than a grey line across the sky.
Devant vous, au-delà des champs en frich: Ahead of you, beyond the fallow fields, a hill covered in vines, and on the hill, a bell tower of pale golden stone. A bell rings there, just once, then falls silent. Someone up there is still keeping the hours.

Samedi. Partis à 6 h pour éviter les bou:
Saturday. Left at 6 a.m. to beat the traffic. Didn’t work. The radio says there’s an accident on the viaduct, then it says something else we can’t understand. Léa threw up her cereal. Tom is counting red lorries.

Saturday evening. We’re not moving at all now. People are getting out of their cars to smoke. The radio says to stay in your vehicles and keep the windows shut. Nobody says why.

Sunday. There was screaming near exit 14. A man ran past, bleeding from the neck. We kept the windows shut. Two bottles of water left and Tom’s packet of biscuits.

Monday. The lady in the Clio in front of us isn’t moving any more. She still has her seatbelt on. She knocks her head against the window, gently, non-stop. I told the children she was sleeping badly.

Tuesday. Léa has a fever. Not that one, I think. I think. Men in orange motorway vests came by with bottles of water. They wanted half our things. I gave them Dad’s watch.

Wednesday. Marc won’t leave on foot. He says we have to wait for help. He won’t leave the car. I don’t understand how anyone can care about a car.

Wednesday night. I’m leaving with the children. I couldn’t find the buckles on the seats in the dark, so I cut the straps. Marc is asleep. I’m leaving him this notebook so he knows where to find us: at my sister’s, in Brennes. Marc, if you read this, come. Leave the car.

La route quitte la vallée et monte entre: The road leaves the valley and climbs between rows of vines no one has pruned for two winters. The canes have grown every which way, knotted themselves from one row to the next, and the whole hillside looks like a head of hair that has never been combed.
Au sommet, un mur de pierre blonde, un c: At the top, a wall of pale golden stone, a square bell tower, tiled roofs. Saint-Aubin Priory. A thin thread of smoke rises from a chimney. Somewhere behind the wall, someone is drawing water from a well: the creak of the pulley carries down to you, regular, unhurried, as if nothing had happened in the world.

“We don’t kill them here. We bring them back. Yours are tied up in the barn; they won’t do anything more to you. Stay lying down.”

FERRAND INSTITUTE — Medical Vessel Destinée

Requisition of technical staff. Pursuant to the Ferrand protocol, agents André Dufour and Paulin Roche are assigned without delay to the maintenance of the vessel. Their families are not covered by this order.

The Vaulx–Morvan line will remain de-energised until further notice, in order to guarantee control of access during sorting at the lock. Any unauthorised re-energising will be considered an act of hostility towards the Institute.

“Good.” From her, that is a speech.

Plus loin, la digue mène à une butte de: Further on, the causeway leads to a mound of solid ground where a few spindly birches huddle round a hut with a tin roof.

Kaz finally comes up, but his left leg was caught under a log, and when he tears it free his trousers are ripped open from knee to ankle. He limps. He says nothing, and that is worse than anything he could have said.

Une partie de ce qui était dans les sacs: Part of what was in the packs stayed down there. The peat gives nothing back.

There are no birds left to disturb.

« Gaspard. Il marche vers l’écluse, lui: “Gaspard. He’s heading for the lock too. It’s all he has left.”

Carry on towards the heart of the marsh.

Sur la table, un carnet à couverture cir: On the table, a notebook with a waxed cover, a dry cup, and a binocular case, open. Empty.
Sous le lit, une caisse : une conserve,: Under the bed, a crate: a tin, a bottle of methylated spirits, rags, an orange distress flare still in its wrapping. On the wall, a map of the marsh. Elle a tourné la tête vers la digue. Ell: She has turned her head towards the causeway. She is looking for you.

Contourner la fosse par les îlots du nor: Skirt the pool by the northern islets, feeling your way, in silence.
Confier la cloche du Berger au courant d: Give the Shepherd’s bell to the current of the southern channel, and let it ring.
La cloche ne vous servira plus à l’éclus: The bell will be no use to you at the lock.

The detour will cost you the morning.

Step onto the narrows and face the Lady of the Bogs and her guard.

D’îlot en îlot, de touffe en touffe, san: From islet to islet, tussock to tussock, with nothing to go by but ground that gives or holds. Twice you put your foot into nothing and pull it back just in time.

Le dernier îlot est le plus proche d’ell: The last islet is the closest to her. There is no other way.
Passer, un pas après l’autre, sans respi: Pass, one step after another, without breathing.

A sucking sound under your sole. Almost nothing. Enough.

The clicking stops. The silence is worse.

Vous l’attachez par un lacet à un bout d: You tie it with a lace to a stub of log and push the log into the channel heading south. The current is almost nothing. Almost.

« À l’écluse, on en aurait peut-être eu: “We might have needed that at the lock.” He shrugs. “We might also have died here.”
La cloche du Berger a emmené la Dame des: The Shepherd’s bell led the Lady of the Bogs away to the south of the marsh.

Le dernier îlot. Puis la digue reprend,: The last islet. Then the causeway resumes on the far side of the pool, and you step onto it the way you step onto a platform. Behind you, the Lady has not moved. She is still waiting for whatever she is waiting for. It was not you.

« Les fossés sont toujours plus vieux qu: “Ditches are always older than marshes. Engineers come and go, the marshes come back, but the ditches remember the plan.” He looks delighted. You cannot see the Lady. You cannot hear her. That is exactly what you wanted.

Vous avez traversé les tourbières sans a: You crossed the bogs without facing the Lady.
Walk towards the edge of the marsh.
À deux mètres, la mousse frémit. La Dame: Two metres away, the moss quivers. The Lady rises with a long sucking sound, and the whole marsh seems to rise with her.
La Dame des tourbières. Sa mousse sèche: The Lady of the Bogs. Her dry moss burns well; watch out when the peat opens beneath your feet.
La Dame se redresse dans un long bruit d: The Lady rises with a long sucking sound. In the front row, one of the Drowned from the causeway turns with her. You let it pass earlier. It was waiting for you.
La Dame des tourbières et un Noyé. Sa mo: The Lady of the Bogs and a Drowned. Her dry moss burns well; don’t let the Drowned hold your ankles.
La tourbe s’ouvre sous vous, et cette fo: The peat opens beneath you, and this time no hand catches you. It is cold, and then it isn’t. The fog closes over the place where you were.

Autour, les Muets restés dans l’eau tour: All around, the Mutes left in the water turn their heads every which way, like people who have just been told the train is not coming. Then, one by one, they scatter into the fog.
Sur la passe, quelque chose est resté ac: On the narrows, something has caught on a root: a leather strap, and at the end of it a pair of binoculars, the lens cracked, full of silt.

« Elle avait l’air de quelqu’un », dit T: “She looked like somebody,” says Théo. No one answers him.
« Paix à elle. Et à mes genoux. »: “Rest in peace. Her and my knees.”
Maëlle vous fait tourner sur vous-même,: Maëlle turns you round, examines your arms, your neck, your hands. No bite. At last she breathes out.
You brought down the Lady of the Bogs.
Le brouillard se lève d’un coup, comme o: The fog lifts all at once, like a sheet being pulled away. Behind you, the marsh becomes what it must have been before: a flat brown heath, rushes, a few birches. You would never guess.
Devant, sur une butte, un village. Des r: Ahead, on a rise, a village. Lorry trailers set end to end as a rampart, sandbags, a bell tower, and smoke rising straight from three chimneys. Cooking smoke. Brennes.
La Dame est au fond de sa fosse. Personn: The Lady is at the bottom of her pool. No one will pass within two metres of her again.
La Dame est toujours là-bas, debout dans: The Lady is still out there, standing in her fog. You think of those walking behind you.
Pour la première fois depuis les Carrièr: For the first time since the Quarries, your pack no longer chimes when you walk.
Sur la route qui longe le village, très: On the road that skirts the village, far off, a lorry is driving towards the river, slowly, without headlights. You cannot see what it is carrying. You know.
Nour s’est assise sur une borne et vide: Nour has sat down on a milestone and is emptying the peat out of her shoes. She counted the whole marsh. She does not say the number.
Carnet à couverture cirée, cabane de l’î: Waxed-cover notebook, islet hut, the bogs
12 mars. Toujours pas de butor. La réser:
12 March. Still no bittern. The reserve has been closed since the Fever, no one will come looking for me, and that suits me fine. I’m staying with the birds.

2 April. First walker on the causeway. A man in oilskins, walking without looking where he put his feet. He fell into the Rush Pool and didn’t come up. This evening I saw him standing in the water, in the same spot, his head level with the reeds. His teeth were chattering.

19 May. There are eleven of them. They all come from the south, along the road. The peat preserves them: they don’t rot, they grow heavier. They follow the sound of water, and anything that chimes. A herd bell at the Morel farm got them all up one morning.

3 July. They gather round the great pool, near the narrows. Standing, motionless, all facing the same point. Like people on a platform waiting for a train.

28 August. Light draws them: at night they follow my lamp. I don’t light it any more. I’ve planted white-painted stakes across the northern islets so I can get home in the dark. Four hundred paces, counting carefully.

14 October. I wanted a closer look. You must never want a closer look. Bite on the forearm. It isn’t deep.

15 October. Fever. I’m going to go down and sit at the edge of the great pool, with the binoculars. At least I’ll finally know what they’re waiting for.

— M. Varenne, reserve warden
Le brouillard des tourbières se déchire: The fog over the bogs tears open all at once, like a curtain being drawn, and there is Brennes: a squat bell tower, slate roofs, and all around a wall made of whatever the road left behind. Lorry trailers laid end to end, sandbags, welded car doors, farm harrows with their teeth turned outwards.
Sur le mur, des silhouettes et des fusil: On the wall, figures and hunting rifles. And, something you have not seen in months, chimney smoke that smells of leeks.
Au-dessus du portail, une banderole pein: Above the gate, a hand-painted banner: “BRENNES — HERE WE HELP EACH OTHER”. The letters have been gone over several times. Someone cares about it.
« Brennes. J’ai fait passer leurs pénich: “Brennes. I used to put their beet barges through the lower lock, back in the day. They had a mayor who talked too much.” He squints at the wall. “Maybe they still have one.”
Nour s’est arrêtée. Elle compte les fusi: Nour has stopped. She counts the rifles under her breath. “Seven.” Then she counts the windows of the town hall, and she does not say why.
Personne ne marche à côté de vous. La fu: No one walks beside you. The chimney smoke tightens your throat more than the fog ever did.
Avancer à découvert jusqu’au portail, le: Walk out in the open up to the gate, hands clearly visible.
[Éclaireur] Se glisser sous le pont du c: [Scout] Slip under the railway bridge, where no one ever looks.
Contourner par le talus de la voie ferré: Circle round by the railway embankment to watch the village before showing yourself.
The railway embankment overlooks the gardens. Flat on your stomach in the brambles, you see everything: vegetable plots laid out with string, a swept school yard, a square with a running fountain. A life. A village.
Et la salle des fêtes, au bout de la pla: And the village hall, at the end of the square: a prefab with its shutters closed in broad daylight, a new padlock on the door. A man sits outside on a kitchen chair, a rifle across his knees. He is not watching the road. He is watching the door.
La porte s’ouvre. Deux adolescents sorte: The door opens. Two teenagers come out to empty a bucket, under escort. A girl of about sixteen, a younger boy. Clean, well fed, hair neatly combed. The boy wears a polo neck despite the midday sun. The girl has a dressing at the base of her neck, where the shoulder begins.
« Elle a un pansement au même endroit qu: “She’s got a dressing in the same place as me,” Théo breathes. His hand has gone up to his shoulder on its own.
Au bout du village, la gare : un quai, u: At the far end of the village, the station: a platform, a cast-iron canopy, a brick shed with a tin roof. The single track runs north alongside the river.
Brennes garde deux adolescents sous clé: Brennes keeps two teenagers locked up in its village hall.
Redescendre et se présenter au portail,: Climb back down and present yourself at the gate, as if nothing had happened.
Le portail est une benne à ordures monté: The gate is a rubbish skip mounted on wheelbarrow wheels. They roll it aside for you. Behind it, a cobbled street, children who fall silent when they see you, and a man coming to meet you with both hands outstretched.
Les sentinelles vous ont vus ramper sur: The sentries saw you crawling on the embankment. They say nothing, but two barrels follow you all the way to the gate, and the smile of the man who greets you arrives half a second after he does.
La soixantaine, un gilet de laine bouton: In his sixties, a wool cardigan buttoned to the top, reading glasses hanging from a cord. He clasps your hand between both of his, for a long time, warmly. While he holds it, his eyes travel round your neck.
« Bertrand Vautrin. Maire de Brennes ava: “Bertrand Vautrin. Mayor of Brennes before, and still now, for want of other candidates.” He laughs at his own joke. “Welcome. Here, we don’t ask people where they come from. We ask them if they’re hungry.”
Il serre ensuite la main de Théo. Plus l: Then he shakes Théo’s hand. For longer. He puts his other hand on the boy’s shoulder, fatherly, and his thumb slides under the collar of the jacket, just a little, just where the scar is. Théo steps back. Vautrin smiles as if nothing had happened.
« Ne le touchez pas. » Maëlle a parlé do: “Don’t touch him.” Maëlle spoke softly. That is worse than if she had shouted.
Il se penche vers Nour, lui demande son: He bends down to Nour, asks how old she is, pinches her cheek. Nour does not answer. She pulls her collar up with a sharp tug, and Vautrin watches her do it very closely.
« Il y a de la soupe à midi, à la cantin: “There’s soup at noon in the school canteen, for everyone. Beds at the town hall for anyone who wants to sleep. A market under the school shelter, if you’ve something to barter. Make yourselves at home.” He pats his cardigan pocket. “Brennes is a family.”
Sur la place, des traces de pneus larges: In the square, wide tyre tracks in the mud, still fresh. A lorry came through this morning. Vautrin follows your gaze. “Hauliers. They never stop for long.”
À Brennes, le maire Vautrin offre la sou: In Brennes, Mayor Vautrin offers soup and beds. He looks at the backs of necks.
Follow the mayor to the square.
La place de Brennes a une fontaine qui c: The square at Brennes has a fountain that really runs, a lime tree, a town hall with blue shutters and, right at the end, the village hall with its new padlock. The market is held under the school shelter: trestles, jars, bicycle parts. People barter in low voices, as if in church.
Vautrin est reparti vers la mairie avec: Vautrin has gone back to the town hall with a pat on your back. Ever since, there has always been someone watching you without seeming to: a man mending a chair, a woman hanging out washing. Always the same ones, changing places.
Le garde de la salle des fêtes ne vous l: The village hall guard never takes his eyes off you now. Vautrin waves to you from afar every time you cross the square. He knows you looked where you shouldn’t have.
Un gamin, à la fontaine, raconte qu’hier: A kid at the fountain says that last night the bulbs in the town hall came back on by themselves for an hour. “Like before.” He says it the way people talk about a miracle. You know which circuit breaker was reset at Vaulx.
Kaz s’est assis sur la margelle de la fo: Kaz has sat down on the rim of the fountain and is looking at the town hall roof. “There’s an aerial up there. A real one, marine radio. That’s a lot for a village of beet farmers.”
Have a look round the market under the shelter.
Entrer dans l’école, d’où monte le bruit: Go into the school, where the sound of a dictation drifts out.
Pousser jusqu’à la gare, au bout du vill: Walk on to the station, at the end of the village.
Se glisser derrière la salle des fêtes p: Slip round behind the village hall while the guard is eating.
Se rendre à la cantine pour la soupe de: Go to the canteen for the midday soup.
Under the shelter, everyone trades what they have. Tins without labels, knitted socks, batteries that might work. An old woman in an apron runs the best-stocked stall: jars of beans, rye loaves, and a shoebox full of dressings.
Elle s’appelle Mme Ribot. Elle a quatre-: Her name is Mme Ribot. She is eighty and sharp as ever, and she talks while keeping an eye on the town hall over your shoulder.
« La soupe de Bertrand est bonne, dit-el: “Bertrand’s soup is good,” she says. “I don’t take it any more. I eat at home. At my age, you sleep quite enough.” She adds nothing. She puts her jars away, one by one, with great care.
« Ce matin, à l’aube, il est passé une d: “This morning, at dawn, a thin woman came through with a little boy who saluted everyone the wrong way, left hand to his forehead. She didn’t want the soup either. She said she knew all about people who are too kind.” Mme Ribot nods. “A sensible woman.”
« Et le camion de ce matin, ajoute-t-ell: “And the lorry this morning,” she adds, lower, “there were cages under the tarpaulin. Bertrand filled it up for them. A boy inside was drawing on the canvas with a nail.” You do not ask what he was drawing. You know.

Deux bandages propres contre une bouteil: Two clean bandages for a bottle of spirits.
Du fil de cuivre et des chiffons contre: Copper wire and rags for a ration.
Quatre cartouches de chasse contre une b: Four shotgun shells for a box of antibiotics.
Demander à Mme Ribot ce que la soupe a d: Ask Mme Ribot what is so special about the soup.
Mme Ribot : « Les jours où il y a des ét: Mme Ribot: “On days when there are strangers, Bertrand brings out the blue pot. On days when there are strangers, there’s always someone who sleeps too much.”
Quatorze enfants dans une classe faite p: Fourteen children in a classroom made for thirty. A dictation on the blackboard, in rounded handwriting: “The river flows to the sea. The sea is big. We will go and see it.” The teacher, a young woman with bitten nails, signals you to wait until the end of the sentence.
Au mur, entre la carte de France et un a: On the wall, between the map of France and an illustrated alphabet, a pinned sheet: “Mayor’s Medical Inspection”. First names, dates, crosses. Almost all the crosses are in pencil. Two are in red ink, and next to those two names, Elsa and Samuel, someone has written: “Boarding”.

Théo s’est assis au fond, sur une chaise: Théo has sat down at the back, on a chair too small for him. He watches the children write. He has not set foot in a classroom for fourteen months. He looks as though something hurts.
« Il y a seize chaises et quatorze enfan: “There are sixteen chairs and fourteen children,” Nour says on the way out. “The two spare chairs still have labels with names on them.”
En vous raccompagnant, la maîtresse parl: As she sees you out, the teacher talks very fast, without looking at you: “They’re better fed than we are, over there. The mayor says they’ll go off and heal the world. He says we should be proud.” She shuts the door before you can answer.
Revenir pendant la récréation et ouvrir: Come back during break and open the drawer of the teacher’s desk.
Dans le tiroir de l’école : le carnet de: In the school drawer: the mayor’s “medical inspection” register. Carrier children are sent off “to board”.
La gare de Brennes est une boîte de briq: Brennes station is a brick box with a clock stopped at eight minutes to twelve, the time, perhaps, when the last train went through. A platform, a cast-iron canopy, a bench. The single track runs north between two bramble-covered embankments, and the river gleams below, wide and slow.
Contre le quai, la remise : briques noir: Against the platform, the shed: blackened bricks, a sliding sheet-metal door, and a railwayman’s padlock with a square barrel, the kind that only opens with a T-key.
Vous sortez la clé d’Armand. Elle entre: You take out Armand’s key. It slides into the barrel like a knife into butter and turns with the clean click of well-greased machinery. In the smell of oil and dust, a low shape under a green tarpaulin. Four iron wheels. A pump handle. The old man had not lied.
Vous refermez aussitôt. Pas maintenant,: You shut it again at once. Not now, not with half the village watching from the square. But you know where it is, and the line starts here.
Vous secouez la porte. Elle ne bouge pas: You shake the door. It does not move a millimetre. Through a gap between two sheets of metal, you can make out a green tarpaulin, a low shape, something on wheels. You would need the key. Or a lot of noise.
