La draisine d’Armand attend sous une bâc: Armand’s handcar waits under a green tarpaulin in the shed at Brennes station.
[Technicien] Débloquer en douce le levie: [Tinkerer] Quietly free the rusted points lever at the end of the platform.
Vous avez dégagé l’aiguillage de la gare: You have freed the station points: through the gardens and along the platform, you can leave Brennes without passing the militiaman.
Derrière la salle des fêtes, une fenêtre: Behind the village hall, a toilet window not properly shut. You push it open with your fingertips.
Deux lits de camp faits au carré, une ta: Two camp beds made with hospital corners, a table, a draughts set, a basket of apples. A poster for the “14 July Dance” still hangs on the wall. The girl from the embankment is reading a paperback. The boy is asleep, or pretending to be. They look healthy. They look as if they are waiting for a train.
Elle lève les yeux. Elle ne crie pas. «: She looks up. She does not scream. “Are you from the barge? You’re early. The mayor said tonight.” Then she sees your face, and she understands you are not.
« Je m’appelle Elsa. Lui, c’est Samuel,: “My name’s Elsa. This is Samuel, my brother. He took us at the Saint-Aubin market, with our parents. Our parents went away with cans of diesel and a crate of medicine. They thought they were doing the right thing. The mayor swore to them the Institute would cure us.” She tugs at her collar: a round white scar at the base of her neck. “We’re not ill. That’s the problem.”
Théo s’est approché de la fenêtre. Il ba: Théo has come up to the window. He pulls down his own collar, slowly, and shows his shoulder. Elsa looks at the crescent of teeth for a long time. No one says anything. There is nothing to say.
Deux porteurs, Elsa et Samuel, sont gard: Two carriers, Elsa and Samuel, are being kept “boarding” in the Brennes village hall. The barge is due to collect them tonight.
Les faire sortir par la fenêtre maintena: Get them out through the window now and hide them at Mme Ribot’s.
Elsa et Samuel sont sortis par la fenêtr: Elsa and Samuel climbed out through the window. Mme Ribot hid them in her cellar, behind the jars, without asking a single question.
Leur dire de se tenir prêts : vous revie: Tell them to be ready: you will come back for them.
Gravel crunches behind you. The village hall guard is there, his plate still in one hand and his rifle in the other. In his forties, a wedding ring, the look of someone who did not choose this job but will do it all the same.
« Les toilettes publiques, c’est à la ma: “The public toilets are at the town hall,” he says. He does not shoot. He whistles, two short notes, and Vautrin comes trotting up, his cardigan buttoned wrong.
« On se perd vite, à Brennes, toutes ces: “It’s easy to get lost in Brennes, all these little streets.” He takes you by the arm, warm and firm. “The village hall is closed for works. Asbestos, you know. We don’t take chances with health here.”
Se laisser raccompagner jusqu’à la place: Let yourself be walked back to the square.
La cantine de l’école sent le poireau, l: The school canteen smells of leeks, potatoes and warm bread. Thirty people on benches, chipped bowls, clinking spoons. For the first time since the Fever, you hear people talking with their mouths full.
Vautrin sert lui-même. Il passe entre le: Vautrin serves in person. He moves between the tables with a ladle and a word for everyone. On the serving hatch, two pots: a large cast-iron one, and a small blue enamel one, set apart on a hotplate.
Quand votre tour vient, il plonge la lou: When your turn comes, he dips the ladle into the blue pot for Théo’s bowl. “For the young man, the best. He needs his strength, at his age.” The other bowls he fills from the big pot, without a thought.
Quand votre tour vient, il remplit le bo: When your turn comes, he fills Nour’s bowl from the blue pot. “For the little miss, the best.” He sets it down in front of her with a wink. The other bowls come from the big one.
Quand votre tour vient, il remplit votre: When your turn comes, he fills your bowl from the blue pot, as he does for no one else in the room. “For our guest, the best.” He stays standing beside you, ladle in hand. “After the meal, a little health check. A formality. We don’t let the Fever into Brennes.”
This time he sits down opposite you. He does not eat. He watches you eat.
La soupe fume. Elle a une odeur de soupe: The soup steams. It smells of soup. Almost.
Laisser Maëlle sentir le bol avant que q: Let Maëlle smell the bowl before anyone touches it.
Écouter Nour, qui vous tire par la manch: Listen to Nour, who is tugging at your sleeve and counting the pots.
[Ancien ambulancier] Tremper le bout de: [Paramedic] Touch the tip of your tongue to it: you know that syrupy taste.
Ne pas toucher à la soupe. Vous en avez: Leave the soup alone. You have seen enough in this village.
Watch what Vautrin himself is eating.
Goûter du bout des lèvres et se fier à s: Taste it with the tip of your lips and trust your palate.
Manger. Vous avez faim, et ces gens ont: Eat. You are hungry, and these people seem so kind.
« Chloral », souffle Maëlle en reposant: “Chloral,” Maëlle breathes, putting the bowl down. “Or a pharmacy sleeping syrup. It smells of overripe pear. We used to give it to the old folk at the hospital so they wouldn’t get up in the night.” She looks at Vautrin. “This one is dosed so you don’t get up at all.”
« Il a servi trente et un bols à la gran: “He served thirty-one bowls from the big pot,” Nour whispers. “Only one from the small one. And he doesn’t eat.”
Le goût vous revient d’un coup, d’avant: The taste comes back to you all at once, from before: overripe pear, the bitterness underneath. The syrup you spooned into agitated patients in the back of the ambulance. This one is dosed for a horse.
Le bol de la marmite bleue a un reflet h: The bowl from the blue pot has an oily sheen and a smell of overripe pear. Leek soup does not smell of pear.
Vous faites semblant. La cuillère monte: You pretend. The spoon goes up and down, and the soup ends up under the table, in the bowl of an old dog that falls asleep almost at once, paws in the air.
Vautrin attend. Il consulte sa montre, u: Vautrin waits. He checks his watch, once, twice. After a quarter of an hour, he nods to two men near the door.
Les deux hommes s’approchent de Théo. Th: The two men approach Théo. Théo watches them come, eyes wide open, and Vautrin’s smile freezes.
Les deux hommes s’approchent de Nour. No: The two men approach Nour. Nour watches them come, sitting very straight on her bench, and says out loud: “I’m not sleepy.” Vautrin’s smile freezes.
« Bien. Ce petit contrôle sanitaire, mai: “Right. That little health check, now. It’ll only take a minute.” A hand lands on your shoulder from behind, and squeezes.
Se lever, lentement, et repousser le ban: Stand up, slowly, and push back the bench.
The spoon grows heavier and heavier. The voices in the canteen stretch out, like a record slowing down. You see Vautrin smile, and you think it a very kind smile, and then you see nothing at all.
Vous revenez à vous avec une bouche de c: You come to with a mouth like cardboard, your forehead on the table. Someone has put a blanket over your shoulders. Outside, the light has shifted.
Deux hommes portent Théo vers la porte,: Two men are carrying Théo towards the door, one under each arm. His feet drag on the tiles. His eyes are half closed, he is looking at you, and he is trying to say your name.
Un homme emporte Nour vers la porte, tou: A man carries Nour towards the door, limp, her plaits hanging down. She opens one eye. She is still counting, under her breath, the steps between her and the way out.
Vous revenez à vous dans le bureau du ma: You come to in the mayor’s office, on a chair, your wrists taped to the armrests. A strip of yellow paper is soaking in a small glass cup with three drops of your blood. Vautrin studies it against the light, his glasses on his nose.
« Elle reste jaune. » Il soupire, sincèr: “It stays yellow.” He sighs, genuinely disappointed. “Pity. Really. Well, the Institute also takes hands for the holds. It pays less, but it’s something.”
« Je ne mange jamais ce que je n’ai pas: “I never eat what I haven’t seen cooked.” Inès is behind you, crossbow loaded under her jacket. She let you sleep while she counted the men. “Four. Get up.”
Se jeter sur eux, la tête encore pleine: Throw yourself at them, your head still full of cotton wool.
Tout se joue sur la place, devant la fon: It all comes to a head in the square, by the fountain, in broad daylight. The people from the canteen have come out, napkins still in hand. Four militiamen form a circle, hunting rifles at the hip, unsure whether to raise them. Vautrin is in the middle, red-faced, out of breath, and still smiling. Smiling is his trade.
Vous tenez debout, mais le sol penche. L: You are on your feet, but the ground tilts. The syrup is still in your veins, heavy and sweet.
Théo est contre vous, une main crispée s: Théo is pressed against you, one hand clenched on your sleeve. He is standing. He is doing it on purpose.
« Allons, allons. Personne ne va se fair: “Come now, come now. No one’s going to get hurt. It’s a misunderstanding.” He spreads his arms towards the crowd. “These people have been walking, they’re tired, they see plots everywhere. We in Brennes protect our children. Go home.”
Personne ne rentre. La maîtresse est là,: No one goes home. The teacher is there, arms folded very tight. Mme Ribot is there, leaning on her stick. They are waiting. They have been waiting for something for a long time, perhaps, without ever knowing what.
« Je connais ces gens, souffle Kaz. Ils: “I know these people,” Kaz breathes. “They’re not wicked. They’re scared. Give them a reason to be less scared of us than of him.”
Brandir l’ordre de mission du convoi et: Hold up the convoy’s mission order and read it aloud.
Faire écouter à la place la voix de Rous: Play Rousset’s voice to the square: “The rest is negotiable.”
Lire la circulaire de l’Institut : « tra: Read the Institute’s circular: “priority transfer of asymptomatic carriers”.
Faire signe à Mme Ribot : qu’elle amène: Signal to Mme Ribot: have her bring Elsa and Samuel to the square.
Envoyer Inès par la fenêtre des toilette: Send Inès in through the village hall toilet window.
Courir à la salle des fêtes, faire saute: Run to the village hall, break the padlock and show everyone what is inside.
[Guerrier] Arracher le fusil du premier: [Fighter] Wrench the rifle from the first militiaman and hold the circle at bay long enough to reach the station.
Profiter de la confusion pour filer vers: Use the confusion to slip away to the station and the railway line.
Le premier milicien lève son fusil. Le c: The first militiaman raises his rifle. The circle tightens. Vautrin backs away behind the fountain, shouting at them to aim for the legs, “the legs, only the legs!” Even now, he is thinking of the merchandise.
Deux miliciens de Brennes, fusils de cha: Two Brennes militiamen, hunting rifles and wool cardigans. They are not killers. They are afraid, and that is what makes them dangerous.
Vous coupez par les potagers, entre les: You cut through the vegetable plots, between rows of leeks and bean poles, bent double under the drying sheets. Behind you, shouts, a whistle, slamming doors. Ahead, the railway embankment and the station canopy.
Kaz porte Théo sur son dos comme un sac: Kaz carries Théo on his back like a sack of grain. Théo’s eyes are open and he does not let go of his neck.
Le milicien du quai a entendu le sifflet: The militiaman on the platform heard the whistle. He has thrown away his cigarette and is waiting, rifle shouldered, at the end of the bench.
Passer par l’aiguillage que vous avez dé: Go through the points you freed, behind the shed, out of his sight.
Ramper le long du talus jusqu’au quai sa: Crawl along the embankment to the platform without being seen.
Ramper le long du talus jusqu’au quai, s: Crawl along the embankment to the platform, under the eyes of a guard who has been expecting you since morning.
Courir droit sur le quai, tant pis pour: Run straight onto the platform, never mind the noise.
Le milicien du quai tire en l’air, puis: The militiaman on the platform fires into the air, then lets loose the station dog, a black griffon that has never seen you and already hates you.
Le milicien du quai et son chien vous ba: The platform militiaman and his dog bar your way to the railway line.
Le ballast crisse sous vos semelles. Der: The ballast crunches under your soles. Behind you, the wall of Brennes closes in on itself: trailers, sandbags, harrows. On the rampart, the figures do not shoot. They watch what they could not hold on to leave.
Personne ne vous suit sur la voie. Un vi: No one follows you along the track. A frightened village does not leave its walls.
Mme Ribot a caché Elsa et Samuel dans sa: Mme Ribot has hidden Elsa and Samuel in her cellar, behind the jars. You will probably never know whether it was enough.
Derrière un cadenas neuf, dans une salle: Behind a new padlock, in a village hall that smells of apples, two teenagers are still waiting for tonight’s barge.
Vous avez fui Brennes par la voie ferrée: You fled Brennes along the railway line.
Reprendre votre souffle au bout du quai,: Catch your breath at the end of the platform, where the river line begins.
Vous revenez à vous dans le fossé, au pi: You come to in the ditch at the foot of the wall, on the railway side. They threw you out the way you put out the rubbish, after emptying your pockets.
Maëlle nettoie l’entaille de votre arcad: Maëlle cleans the cut over your eyebrow with a corner of rag. One of her eyes is swelling too. “They didn’t dare keep us,” she says. “They didn’t even dare kill us. They’re shopkeepers.”
Théo est assis sur un rail, entier. Il a: Théo is sitting on a rail, unharmed. He has his knees under his chin and is looking at the wall. No one took him. It is the afternoon’s only victory, and the only one that counts.
Sur le rempart, le garde de la salle des: On the rampart, the village hall guard watches you get up. He hesitates, then lobs a jar of beans over the sandbags; it rolls to your feet without breaking.
Rossés par la milice de Brennes et jetés: Beaten by the Brennes militia and thrown out of the walls.
Se relever et marcher jusqu’au quai de l: Get up and walk to the station platform, outside the wall.
Vous lisez lentement. « Collecte de port: You read slowly. “Collection of carriers, Valombre-North sector. Priority: young subjects.” You read the signature. Then you hand the laminated sheet to the teacher, who reads it in turn and passes it to her neighbour. It goes round the square, from hand to hand, bloodstained, and each hand trembles a little more than the last.
Le dictaphone grésille au milieu du sile: The dictaphone crackles in the middle of the silence. Rousset’s voice comes out of it, metallic, tiny: “The protocol provides for the carriers. The rest is negotiable.” You rewind. You play it a second time. On the second, a militiaman lowers his rifle.
Vous lisez la circulaire de l’Institut,: You read out the Institute’s circular, its “Confidential” stamp, its sentences as clean as ironed sheets: “identification”, “transfer”, “asymptomatic carriers”. No one in Brennes had ever seen those words written down. They all look at their mayor.
Elsa et Samuel traversent la place en cl: Elsa and Samuel cross the square, blinking in the sunlight. Elsa pulls down her collar in front of everyone. The scar is there, round and white. “He told our parents the Institute would cure us. We’re not ill. We’re for sale.” Her voice does not tremble. It is Samuel’s that trembles, behind her.
Vautrin ouvre la bouche. Rien ne sort. P: Vautrin opens his mouth. Nothing comes out. For the first time, he cannot find the kind word.
C’est Mme Ribot qui parle. « Bertrand. M: It is Mme Ribot who speaks. “Bertrand. My grandson Lucas. You told us he’d gone to the Institute to be treated. Lucas wasn’t ill.” She does not shout. No one shouts. Someone takes the rifle from a militiaman’s hands, gently, the way you take a knife from a child.
« Je t’ai connu, Vautrin, quand tu venda: “I knew you, Vautrin, when you sold your beets by weight with your thumb on the scales.” Kaz spits on the ground. “You haven’t changed trades.”
Théo, à côté de vous, a remis son col en: Théo, beside you, has put his collar back in place. He looks at Vautrin without hatred. That is worse.
Une heure plus tard, Bertrand Vautrin qu: An hour later, Bertrand Vautrin leaves Brennes on foot through the skip gate, a suitcase in his hand, his wool cardigan buttoned to the top. No one hits him. No one says goodbye. In the school, the teacher takes down the medical inspection sheet and burns it in the stove.
Le village vous remplit les sacs sans qu: The village fills your packs without being asked: rye bread, beans, clean bandages. Mme Ribot takes your face between her dry hands and says nothing at all.
Reste la radio de la mairie, et son ante: There is still the town hall radio, and its marine aerial. Tonight, the barge is expecting a call from Brennes.
Brennes a chassé son maire. Elsa et Samu: Brennes has driven out its mayor. Elsa and Samuel will not be handed over to the barge.
Fouiller le bureau de Vautrin avant que: Search Vautrin’s office before someone else does.
Dans le bureau de Vautrin : le bordereau: In Vautrin’s office: the Destinée’s supply slip. Two carriers in exchange for diesel, antibiotics and six places on board, his own among them.
Arracher les lampes de la radio : que Ro: Rip the valves out of the radio: let Rousset think Brennes is his until dawn.
Brennes will not be able to call anyone again.
Vous avez réduit au silence la radio de: You silenced the Brennes radio. On the barge, they are still waiting for the delivery.
Laisser la maîtresse appeler la barge et: Let the teacher call the barge and say that Brennes will hand over no one else.
Le capitaine Rousset saura que quelqu’un: Captain Rousset will know that someone is undoing his deals.
Brennes a prévenu la barge par radio : p: Brennes warned the barge by radio: no more deliveries. Rousset knows.
La lumière a pris la couleur du blé. Au: The light has turned the colour of wheat. At the end of the platform, someone has wound the station clock, and it starts again, months late. The village is behind you, its fountain, its canteen, its school where they write that we will go and see the sea.
Dans le micro de la mairie, la maîtresse: Into the town hall microphone, the teacher spoke in a clear voice: “This is Brennes. We will hand over no one.” A long silence, then a man’s voice, curt: “Received.” Rousset knows now that someone is walking towards him, undoing what he buys.
Dans la mairie, la radio n’est plus qu’u: In the town hall, the radio is now just an empty box. At the lock, Rousset still believes Brennes will deliver two children to him tonight. He will wait.
Vous mangez assis sur le quai, les jambe: You eat sitting on the platform, legs dangling over the rails, with what Brennes let you take. The village wall looks smaller from here. A wall only protects you from what comes from outside.
Dans votre dos, la remise d’Armand, sa p: Behind you, Armand’s shed, its tin door, its green tarpaulin. Ahead, the river line runs north, two gleaming rails that meet in the distance, at the exact spot where you need to go.
Devant, la ligne du fleuve file vers le: Ahead, the river line runs north between its bramble embankments. Two rails, ballast, and a great many kilometres. The station shed stays shut on its tarpaulined shape.
Le camion du matin a pris la route du gu: The morning lorry took the road to the ford. The rails run alongside it. Somewhere ahead, Théo is drawing on a tarpaulin with a nail.
Théo a sorti son carnet. Il dessine Bren: Théo has taken out his notebook. He is drawing Brennes: the wall, the fountain, the village hall. On the door of the hall, he does not draw a padlock.

MAYOR’S INSPECTIONS — SINGLE CLASS
Check of neck and shoulders. Three drops of blood on a test strip (supplied by the Institute). Yellow: nothing. Blue: “to be reported”.

— Lucas R., 13. Blue. Left for the Institute on 3 March “to be treated”.
— Camille D., 9. Yellow.
— Hugo and Léna P., 7 and 11. Yellow.
— Elsa M., 16, and Samuel M., 12, arrived from Saint-Aubin. Both blue. Boarding.
— (eleven other lines, all yellow)

At the bottom of the page, in rounded handwriting, in pencil, then crossed out: “Blue means they leave. I don’t know where. I don’t know whether I should tell the parents to hide their children’s shoulders. I don’t know whether I’m a coward or just careful.”
INSTITUT FERRAND — NAVIRE MÉDICAL DESTIN:
FERRAND INSTITUTE — MEDICAL VESSEL DESTINÉE
Supply Agreement no. 4 — Commune of Brennes (M. B. Vautrin, mayor)

Subject: two (2) asymptomatic carrier subjects, in satisfactory health, to be handed over to the collection team at the Brennes station platform, on the eve of departure, at nightfall.

Consideration: 400 litres of diesel; one crate of antibiotics; boarding priority for six (6) residents designated by the mayor.

For Captain A. Rousset, the collection chief.

On the back, in biro, in Vautrin’s hand: “Designated: me, Mireille, my brother Georges, his wife, the two little ones. Do not mention to the council. The village will manage perfectly well without us.”
La gare de Brennes tient en trois choses: Brennes station comes down to three things: a brick platform with grass pushing up between the joints, a clock stopped at an hour nobody looks at any more, and, backed against the embankment, the track workers’ shed. A plank door painted oxblood red. A square padlock, the kind that only opens with a railwayman’s key.
Au-delà du heurtoir, la voie unique file: Beyond the buffer stop, the single track runs east between two hedges of brambles. It follows the river all the way to Morvan. Nothing has run on it since the Fever. The rails have taken on the colour of dead leaves.

Ma Mathilde,\n\nLa digue a lâché le soir:
My Mathilde,

The dyke gave way on the evening of Martinmas. I heard it from here, like a door slamming a long way off. By morning, the orchard was a lake. The Reinettes at the bottom have water up to their first branches, the Belchards too. The old Calvilles, the ones your grandfather grafted, are on the mound. They’re holding.

There are things in the water. The Rabiers, the Morels, others I don’t recognise. They never come up onto the mound. I think they’ve forgotten how to climb. I don’t go down to the cellar any more.

Don’t come. I know you’d want to come. There are no more trains anyway, and you have the little ones.

I’m staying with the trees. They’ll blossom in April, there’ll be no one to prune them, and they’ll blossom anyway. That comforts me more than it should.

If someone reads this letter before you do: there are dried apples in the jar, take them. Leave the chair in front of the window.

Your dad,
Gaston Garnier

“Visit from the Ferrand Institute. A captain and six men in grey. Ask us to cut the Morvan line, ‘for health reasons’. Refused. The lock needs its sluices, and so do the river people.”

“They came back. Removed the fuse from the Morvan feeder themselves. Took it away. The captain says a lock with no power can be held with four men. He wants the gates to open only when he decides.”

“They took Dédé and Paulin ‘for maintenance on the barge’. I’m staying. Someone has to stay.”

“The spares are in the store, gallery −2. The water has been up since the March flood, and there are things down there. I won’t go down alone. If anyone reads this: 63 kV, porcelain, third shelf. Isolator first, always. — L. M.”
12 mars. Toujours pas de butor. La réser:
12 March. Still no bittern. The reserve has been closed since the Fever, no one will come looking for me, and that suits me fine. I’m staying with the birds.

2 April. First walker on the causeway. A man in oilskins, walking without looking where he put his feet. He fell into the Rush Pool and didn’t come up. This evening I saw him standing in the water, in the same spot, his head level with the reeds. His teeth were chattering.

19 May. There are eleven of them. They all come from the south, along the road. The peat preserves them: they don’t rot, they grow heavier. They follow the sound of water, and anything that chimes. A herd bell at the Morel farm got them all up one morning.

3 July. They gather round the great pool, near the narrows. Standing, motionless, all facing the same point. Like people on a platform waiting for a train.

28 August. Light draws them: at night they follow my lamp. I don’t light it any more. I’ve planted white-painted stakes across the northern islets so I can get home in the dark. Four hundred paces, counting carefully.

14 October. I wanted a closer look. You must never want a closer look. Bite on the forearm. It isn’t deep.

15 October. Fever. I’m going to go down and sit at the edge of the great pool, with the binoculars. At least I’ll finally know what they’re waiting for.

— Mme Varenne, reserve warden
